lesson.title: Why Angles Aren't Always Ideal: The Fine Print of Molecular Shape
lesson.summary: Bond angles are the measured angles between adjacent bonds at a central atom, and while VSEPR predicts clean idealized values, real molecules deviate in small, predictable ways once lone pairs and multiple bonds enter the picture.
lesson.body:
A bond angle is the angle formed between two bonds that share a common central atom, measured in degrees, and it is one of the most directly measurable pieces of evidence for a molecule's shape, obtainable through techniques like microwave spectroscopy or X ray diffraction. Every molecular geometry covered so far comes with its own idealized bond angle or set of angles: 180 degrees for linear, 120 degrees for trigonal planar, 109.5 degrees for tetrahedral, a combination of 90, 120, and 180 degrees for trigonal bipyramidal, and 90 and 180 degrees for octahedral. These idealized values assume that every electron domain around the central atom is identical, exerting exactly the same amount of repulsion as every other domain.

Real molecules rarely meet that assumption perfectly, and the deviations follow a consistent, predictable order of repulsion strength: lone pair to lone pair repulsion is strongest, lone pair to bonding pair repulsion is next, and bonding pair to bonding pair repulsion is weakest. This ordering comes directly from how tightly each type of domain is held. A bonding pair is pulled by two nuclei at once and stays relatively compact, while a lone pair is held by only one nucleus and spreads into a broader angular region, crowding its neighbors more forcefully and compressing the angles between them.

The clearest demonstration of this trend comes from comparing three molecules built on the same tetrahedral electron geometry but with different numbers of lone pairs. Methane, with zero lone pairs on carbon, sits at the ideal 109.5 degrees. Ammonia, with one lone pair on nitrogen, compresses to about 107 degrees. Water, with two lone pairs on oxygen, compresses further to about 104.5 degrees. Each additional lone pair adds one more source of strong lone pair to bonding pair repulsion, and the measured angle drops accordingly, a clean, stepwise illustration of the repulsion hierarchy in action.

Multiple bonds cause a related but distinct kind of distortion. A double or triple bond packs more electron density into its single domain than an ordinary single bond does, which gives it slightly greater repulsive strength against its neighboring domains, even though it still counts as only one domain for VSEPR purposes. Formaldehyde, H2CO, shows this clearly: carbon has a trigonal planar electron geometry with three domains, one C to O double bond and two C to H single bonds, and the ideal angle for that geometry is 120 degrees. But because the C to O double bond domain repels the two C to H domains a bit more strongly than an ordinary single bond would, the measured H to C to H angle comes in slightly below ideal, around 116 degrees, while the two H to C to O angles open up slightly above 120 degrees to compensate.

These small, systematic deviations are not a failure of VSEPR theory, they are some of its strongest supporting evidence. The idealized angles give a correct starting prediction based purely on the steric number, and the direction and rough size of every deviation, whether from lone pairs or from multiple bonds, follows logically from the same repulsion based reasoning that predicted the base shape in the first place. Measuring a real bond angle and finding it shifted in exactly the direction VSEPR's repulsion hierarchy predicts is a direct, quantitative confirmation that the theory is describing something physically real about how electron domains actually behave around a central atom.
